Case Report
he patient is a 64-year-old man with anti-GAD-antibodypositive SPS who presented with severe chin-on-chest
deformity. He described a progressive history of severe neck pain
over 1 year and weight loss. With reported multiple, daily episodic spasm events over several decades, the patient developed a
severe neck flexion contracture. His deformity prevented him
from having normal respiratory function. He had a medical
history significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia in remis Physical Examination and Imaging
He presented with a chin-on-chest deformity. His neck could
be passively extended 20° to partial horizontal gaze, but he was
unable to maintain. To achieve global sagittal balance and
horizontal gaze, the patient had significant lumbar lordosis,
retroverted pelvis, and flexed knee posture. Muscle strength of
the upper and lower extremities was graded as 5/5 bilaterally.
He had excellent grip and no interosseus atrophy. His gait was
normal.

Imaging displayed severe degenerative disease, spondylolisthesis of C2-C3, C3-C4, and C4-C5. Cervical kyphosis
measured 50°, cervicothoracic kyphosis measured 70°, and
C2-C7 sagittal vertical axis (SVA) of 92. 7 mm. T5 and below
was essentially normal (Figs. 1-A and 1-B). Flexion-extension
radiographs demonstrated fixed spondylolisthesis, but C2-C7
improved to 40° and C2-T2 to 50° (Figs. 1-C and 1-D).
Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated autofusion of
the posterior elements at C3-C4 bilaterally (Figs. 2-A and
2-B). Magnetic resonance imaging showed severe central
canal stenosis at C2-C4, but no spinal cord signal changes
(Figs. 2-C and 2-D).
Treatment and Recovery
Nonoperative treatment proved unsuccessful, and because of
progression of cervical kyphosis, inability to maintain horizontal gaze, and pain, surgical intervention was discussed.
Initial concern was his weight loss, addressed through nutritional evaluation and dietary modifications, allowing him to

gain 7. 3 kg. Anesthesia and pulmonology consults were obtained
for airway assessment and optimization. The neurology service
was consulted for plasmapheresis and IVIG. A pain management consultation was obtained to modify the patient’s pain
requirements and establish protocols for hospitalization. Internal medicine and cardiology consultations were used for optimization and management.
After 3 months of optimization, he underwent surgical
correction of his kyphotic deformity. A posterior-only approach
was determined by many preoperative considerations. For cervicothoracic deformities, our approach is based on several variables
including patient characteristics, fixed versus flexible deformity,
and severity/location. The more severe and fixed a deformity, the
more likely for a combined approach. The less involved levels and
severity of deformity, the more likely for an anterior approach. In
this patient, a combined approach was considered, but because of
the history of neck radiation and previously operated-on tissues,
the senior surgeon decision was to avoid an anterior approach.
After intubation and administration of systemic muscle relaxants,

we reassessed the flexibility of the cervical spine while supine
using intraoperative fluoroscopy. We found reasonable correction
from the simple supine position, confirming that an anterior
approach was not necessary.
From the posterior approach, laminectomies were made
from C1-C7 and T1-T6. Using intraoperative CT-guided stereotactic navigation, posterior instrumentation was placed from
occiput-T6 through a combination of lateral mass screws at
C1, C3-C6 and pedicle screws at C2, C7-T6. Modified Smith Peterson facet osteotomies were performed bilaterally at C2-T1,
which provided enough sagittal correction to attain acceptable
global realignment. It is the senior authors’ opinion to perform

multilevel Smith-Peterson osteotomies for gradual mobilization as opposed to sharp angular pedicle subtraction osteotomies for severe cervical nonrigid kyphotic deformities.
The greatest area of focal kyphosis resided in the level of the
C3-C4 spondylolisthesis. Because of the high morbidity of
upper cervical spine osteotomies, we decided not to perform a
pedicle subtraction osteotomy. Once instrumentation was
placed from occiput-T6, a combination of cervical traction,
manual manipulation of the cranium (through the Mayfield
head holder), and cantilever rod reduction was used to deliver
maximum lordotic correction (Fig. 3). After final correction
and instrumentation, the fusion was augmented with locally
harvested bone graft, allograft frozen crushed cancellous
bone, and bone morphogenic protein. Estimated blood loss
was 1 liter, and he received 5 units of packed red blood cells
and 500cc of cell-saver blood products. He was placed into a
soft collar and transferred to the intensive care unit intubated
and in stable condition.
He was started on a complex pain regimen and extubated
on postoperative day (POD) 1. The patient remained sedated
until POD3, and a feeding tube was placed. On POD4, he was
able to get out of bed and stand and on POD7 walked 243
meters. He started an oral diet on POD11 and discharged home
on POD14.
At the patient’s 1-month postoperative visit, he was doing
well with upright posture, maintained forward gaze, and no
neurological changes. At his 2-month visit, his pain improved
and was ambulating up to 1. 6 km without his walker. Imaging
showed maintained sagittal positioning and no hardware complications (Fig. 4). He was subsequently admitted for revision

right total hip arthroplasty revision at approximately 3 months
postoperatively, due to suspected acetabular polyethylene failure,
and was discharged on POD7.
At his 1-year spinal fusion postoperative visit, he was
able to stand more upright with better forward gaze. Imaging
showed intact hardware with maintained sagittal alignment,
with lordosis of the cervical spine measuring 18° and C2-C7
SVA of 78. 7 mm (Fig. 5). All patient-reported outcomes scores
improved from his preoperative state (visual analog scale,
Oswestry Disability Index, neck disability index, and Short Form
Survey-12), and his clinical pictures demonstrate improved sagittal
alignment (Fig. 6).

This case was complicated by many factors. Patients
with SPS traditionally have a feeling of early satiety, and in this
patient, combined with his xerostomia, severely diminished

his nutritional status. In addition, this is the only case of SPS
we could find that relied heavily on opioid use to control
spasms. This population is highly heterogeneous and a
treatment algorithm may not suit every patient, thus the
importance of a multidisciplinary approach. In addition to
our surgical team, 5 other specialties were involved, including
internal medicine, anesthesia, pulmonology, cardiology, and
pain management, all of which had vital roles in the patient’s
treatment. The generalizability of this case lies within this multiteam approach, which can be used to treat other phenotypic
presentations within the various forms of SPS. Finally, the level of
deformity and surgical approach are risk factors for complications. The decision to only undergo posterior spinal fusion was
made preoperatively and confirmed intraoperatively, as our surgical goals were to achieve improved sagittal balance and avoid an
anterior approach through irradiated, previously operated-on soft
tissues and critical structures. Had we decided intraoperatively
that another approach was necessary, we would have staged his
fixation, with both anterior and posterior approaches.

We
describe a case of SPS in the setting of extreme spinal disease
and deformity. The importance of this case lies in the dramatic
progression of disease, multiteam approach, surgical decisionmaking, and successful outcome, all of which are present
within the first postoperative year. With strict attention to
detail, we show that spinal deformity correction through posterior spinal fusion is possible and can provide quality outcomes for the patient. n
